learningObjective: Choose a robust statistic (median or a percentile) rather than mean when reporting kernel latency in the presence of outliers.

canonicalClaims.claim: Latency distributions are typically right-skewed with sparse outliers; the median (or a trimmed mean) is more representative of steady-state behavior than the arithmetic mean, and tail percentiles (p95/p99) are essential for tail-sensitive workloads.
conditions: Goal is to summarize typical steady-state performance.
nonImplications: Does not imply mean is worthless; for throughput calculations it can be appropriate.
Does not imply p99 is meaningless; it is essential for SLOs but not as a stand-alone summary.

misconceptions.claim: Mean is always the standard summary statistic.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Mean is not robust to right-skewed distributions common in latency.

misconceptions.claim: p99 from 20 samples is a stable statistic.
misconceptions.whyWrong: With small N, extreme percentiles are dominated by 1-2 samples and are noisy.

misconceptions.claim: std deviation is a full percentile encoder under normality.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Latency distributions are typically not normal; the assumption fails.
Even post-warmup, page faults, GC and driver events can produce outliers.
